title: After Astros shake-up, Jim Crane unpacks Dana Brown’s ousting: ‘We expect better’
content:
NEW YORK — No one outcome doomed Dana Brown. He oversaw a disappointing homestand that cost the Houston Astros their American League West lead, but Brown’s fate as the team’s general manager had been sealed long before the ballclub blew a six-run lead on Sunday afternoon against the lowly Athletics.

That it turned out to be Brown’s final game as Houston’s GM is something of a coincidence. Owner Jim Crane said the collapse and catastrophic homestand “didn’t have anything to do with it.” There is no right time to fire someone, Crane said, but the Astros “weren’t where we wanted to be,” forcing the 72-year-old owner to act.

“We expect better,” Crane said on Tuesday afternoon from the bowels of Yankee Stadium, where he traveled to meet the team after a chaotic Monday morning.

Crane conducted a closed-door meeting with manager Joe Espada, during which he reiterated that Espada will guide the club for the remainder of the regular season. Espada, like Brown, entered the season without a contract for next year.

“I told him we’d deal with that at the end of the season,” Crane said. “We’ve never changed that answer all year long.”

Espada, Crane said, is “doing what he can do with what he’s got.”

“You get three or four starters down, you got to really scramble,” he said. “He’s a good manager. He keeps an eye on things. I just talked to him and he’s ready to win a game today.”

Crane exited Espada’s office at Yankee Stadium at 4:13 p.m. ET. Five minutes later, senior adviser Jeff Bagwell entered for his own conversation with Espada. Bagwell will be influential in aiding the Astros during their baseball operations transition, along with assistant general managers Charles Cook, Gavin Dickey and Connor Huff.

Crane will oversee all four men.

“I let the guys do their job,” Crane said. “If they need help, I’m there to help. I sit in the meetings so I can understand what they’re doing sometimes, but we’ve got three good assistant GMs that know what they’re doing and we’ve got Jeff (Bagwell) there. I’ve learned a lot from him over the years. I’ve just got to help when I can.”

Crane said the team will “take our time” in identifying Brown’s replacement. Moving on from Brown when they did will allow the Astros time to vet candidates, though Crane didn’t divulge specific qualities he will look for in a new general manager. Twice, though, Crane said he plans to study the operations of “some pretty good teams that don’t have big payrolls.”

“I think we’ll need to make some adjustments (and) look at how other people do things,” Crane said.

“We still have a chance to win the division and get this team on track. This year, (there’s) a lot of injuries in the pitching and we got off to a slow start. That hurt us. I think you can look at all of it. We’re not where we want to be, but we have a good chance to win the division.”

Crane demands nothing less. He reiterated on Tuesday “the expectation that I have is we’re in the playoffs every year.” Brown did have this ballclub in position to fulfill that edict, but perhaps only due to its place in the American League West, where no team entered Tuesday above .500.

Houston fell one game below .500 after being outscored 54-37 during a nine-game homestand that featured three struggling division rivals: the Seattle Mariners, Los Angeles Angels and the Athletics. Winning more than three of those games may have lessened some scrutiny on Brown, but it wouldn’t have built up enough goodwill to change what Crane ultimately had in mind.

“I think we just needed a change,” Crane said. “We weren’t where we wanted to be. Dana did a good job in a lot of areas and it was just time to move on.”

Brown entered this season on borrowed time. Little about what transpired in April or May — when the Astros stumbled to a 27-34 start — bolstered his case. Nor did brutal performances from the six pitchers Brown added this winter to the major-league roster or the offensive performance of an outfield he failed to adequately address.

Crane still allowed Brown to oversee both the amateur draft — which is Brown’s specialty — and a trade deadline that underwhelmed both fans and figures inside Houston’s clubhouse. Asked whether he considered moving on from Brown before either event, Crane replied “not really, no.”

“I think once all of that was done, we just took a hard look at it,” said Crane, who dismissed Brown 21 days after the trade deadline.

Crane framed the timing as beneficial for Brown, who said in a statement on Monday that he would “look forward to the future as I continue my 36-plus years in professional baseball.” Crane described his final discussion with Brown as “tough,” but that the 59-year-old executive “was very professional and he handled it accordingly.”

Espada said he phoned Brown on Monday afternoon to thank him for their three-year partnership and the opportunity to manage in the major leagues. Brown picked Espada, long a bridesmaid in many other managerial searches, to succeed Dusty Baker after the 2023 season.

“It was tough,” Espada said. “It was a tough conversation. But he was grateful for the opportunity, I’m grateful for our relationship and how we grinded through this together.”

Now, Espada must embark on a 31-game stretch with seismic expectations, both for his own future and that of this franchise.
